newsitem.title: USA: Sumitomo probes grind on despite plea.
newsitem.headline: Sumitomo probes grind on despite plea.

text.p: News that Sumitomo Corp's former top copper trader, Yasuo Hamanaka, planned to plead guilty to fraud charges in Japan drew little comment from U.S. regulators on Tuesday.

"We have no specific statement," Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) spokesman David Gary said. "Our investigation is proceeding on course." Earlier, Britain's Serious Fraud Office issued a similiar statement.
But attorneys and former regulators said a Hamanaka guilty plea could complicate the task of CFTC in trying to unravel the scandal which cost Sumitomo $2.6 billion.
"The Japanese do have a way of insulating themselves from what's happening," former CFTC general counsel Howard Schneider said. "The don't have to be terribly cooperative."
Sumitomo officials and Japanese regulators have been cooperating with the various international probes, but that could come to a halt if the expected plea marks the end of the domestic investigation.
Hamanaka's attorney said the disgraced trader was not trying to manipulate world copper prices, a possible violation of the U.S. Commodity Exchange Act.
And Sumitomo officials have said Hamanaka was acting without proper authority from his superiors.
Still, some attorneys warned against drawing too many conclusions from the possible plea.

"It's all very speculative at this point, but you could see a freezing up if (Hamanaka) pleads guilty," a futures attorney in Washington said. "On the other hand, if things are far along and evidence has been gathered there might too much momentum to stop things."
And higher level political officials could get involved if U.S. regulators felt stymied, Schneider noted.
"At some point if there isn't cooperation, I assume it goes up to the ministerial level, to the State Department," Schneider said.
If the Sumitomo portion of inquiry is deflected, the CFTC might still pursue U.S. firms and banks involved in the copper trading scandal.

Commissioner Joseph Dial said in London this week that the inquiry is concerned not only with possible illicit manipulation of copper prices but also other violations of U.S. law that he did not specify. Dial predicted the inquiry would drag on for some time.
U.S. Attorneys office issued subpoenas to Global Minerals and Metals Corp of New York concerning its copper market dealings.

And several U.S. banks engaged in derivatives transactions with Sumitomo, effectively lending $1 billion to Hamanaka. The CFTC wants to be sure the over-the-counter derivatives transactions were not in violation of laws barring off-exchange trading of futures, sources familiar with the investigation have said.
